findings.claim: “The roles reverse completely during elbow extension (the downward phase of a press-up): the triceps becomes the agonist”
findings.truth: The downward phase of a press-up is elbow FLEXION. Elbow extension is the upward phase, where the triceps is the agonist.
findings.evidence: joint movement definitions in this unit's L3 (flexion = decreasing the joint angle); spec 3.1.1.1 flexion/extension at the elbow.

findings.claim: Key Fact: “First class — Fulcrum between Load and Effort (FLE / EFL).”
findings.truth: If the fulcrum is in the middle the letter order is LFE (or EFL). FLE puts the fulcrum at one end and is the SECOND-class order used two lines later. A student copying FLE onto a first-class diagram loses the labelling mark.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.2.1 (positions of fulcrum, load and effort); internal contradiction with the same box's 'first class has F in the middle'.

findings.claim: Worked example: “Imagine a simplified model of the elbow during plantar flexion (second class lever). The effort arm (heel to Achilles insertion) measures 6 cm. The load arm (heel to ankle joint) measures 4 cm.”
findings.truth: Plantar flexion happens at the ankle, not the elbow. Both lever arms must be measured from the fulcrum, which in this lever is the ball of the foot, not the heel (the heel is where the effort acts).
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.2.1 (mechanical advantage = effort arm / resistance arm, arms measured from the fulcrum); the lesson's own second-class description names the ball of the foot as the fulcrum. Arithmetic 6 / 4 = 1.5 recomputed and unchanged.

findings.claim: data-revision-tip: “... second class FLswitchE (F-L-E becomes F at one end, E at other, L between F and E), third class FEL — actually: first=FLE, second=FLE with L between F and E, third=FEL. Try again with the mnemonic FLE/FLE/FEL.”
findings.truth: Generation residue. The tip contradicts itself, is unusable as a revision prompt, and repeats the wrong FLE order for first class.
findings.evidence: internal incoherence; spec 3.1.2.1 lever component order.

findings.claim: “The mark scheme specifically requires the correct LFE arrangement to be visible on any diagram question.”
findings.truth: Invented mark-scheme requirement, and 'LFE arrangement' is not universal — only first-class levers are LFE. The spec asks students to draw a linear lever with the fulcrum, load and effort placed correctly for that class.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.2.1; house rule on board mark-scheme wording.

findings.claim: “A cricket bowler's bowling arm rotates at the shoulder during delivery ... Throwing a javelin involves circumduction of the shoulder.”
findings.truth: Cricket bowling is the spec-named shoulder action and the standard example of circumduction (the arm sweeps a full circle). A javelin throw is an over-the-shoulder pull, not circumduction. The two examples are the wrong way round.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.2.1 additional information: 'shoulder action during cricket bowling', listed against circumduction of the shoulder.

findings.claim: Ruler Drop Test: “A ruler is held by a partner at 0 cm” and mark scheme “partner holds ruler at the 0 cm end”
findings.truth: The partner holds the TOP of the ruler; the 0 cm mark sits level with the top of the performer's open hand, so the reading at the catch point is the distance the ruler fell. Holding the 0 cm end at the top makes the recorded score meaningless.
findings.evidence: standard Ruler Drop (Nelson hand reaction) protocol; spec 3.1.3.2 requires knowledge of the main procedures of the named tests.

findings.claim: Worked example: a 100m sprinter needs “(4) muscular endurance — to sustain near-maximal effort for the full 10–12 seconds”
findings.truth: Muscular endurance is defined in this same lesson as repeated contractions over a long period without tiring. A 10–12 second sprint is not muscular endurance; the sprinter relies on reaction time, power, speed and coordination.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.3.2 component definitions; internal contradiction with the lesson's own definition.

findings.claim: data-revision-tip mnemonic: “3 body-composition/endurance (cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, flexibility)”
findings.truth: Body composition is not a component of fitness on this specification (it belongs to Edexcel and OCR). Naming it in the memory aid invites students to list an eleventh, non-examinable component.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.3.2 lists exactly ten components; body composition does not appear.

findings.claim: “Mo Farah, for example, is reported to have had a resting heart rate in the low 40s during the peak of his marathon career.”
findings.truth: An unverifiable personal physiological statistic attributed to a named athlete, and the framing is wrong: Farah's peak was as a track distance runner, not as a marathon runner. The preceding sentence already gives the correct 35–50 bpm range for elite endurance athletes.
findings.evidence: no source found for the figure and the WebSearch budget is exhausted, so the invented specific is removed rather than corrected.

findings.claim: “The mark scheme rewards all six, so always aim for a wider range.” and “... would place you in the top band.”
findings.truth: Fabricated mark-scheme and band claims. The six functions are on the specification; no board mark scheme is known or quoted here.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.1.1 functions of the skeleton; house rule on board mark-scheme wording.

findings.claim: “Mark schemes award marks for the complete picture: agonist named (1), antagonist named (1), action described at the correct joint (1).”
findings.truth: Invented mark allocation. The advice itself is sound and is kept, but it must not be presented as a board mark scheme.
findings.evidence: house rule on board mark-scheme wording.

findings.claim: “Mark schemes reward a balanced argument with sporting examples on both sides.”
findings.truth: Fabricated mark-scheme attribution; rewritten as advice in the house voice.
findings.evidence: house rule on board mark-scheme wording.

findings.claim: “Examiners reward a balanced argument ...” and, in content_html, “this is exactly the justification examiners look for.”
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claims; rewritten as advice in the house voice.
findings.evidence: house rule on board mark-scheme wording.

findings.claim: Q: “What is the femur and where is it found?” A: “Femur.”
findings.truth: The answer restates the term and answers neither half of the question. The lesson defines the femur as the long bone from hip to knee.
findings.evidence: lesson glossary entry for femur; spec 3.1.1.1 (hip – pelvis and femur; knee – femur and tibia).

findings.claim: KC 2: “one rep max of 100 kg ... for a muscular endurance session, what is the maximum weight she should use?” Options: 80 kg / 70 kg / 65 kg / Just under 70 kg; correct index 3.
findings.truth: The keyed answer is right for the word 'maximum', but the 65 kg distractor is also below 70% of one rep max, so it is defensible for a student reading quickly. Options: (a) leave it, since 'maximum' disambiguates; (b) replace the 65 kg distractor with a value above 70 kg, for example 75 kg, so only one option satisfies the rule. Recommend (b).
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.3.4 (muscular endurance – below 70% of one rep max).
findings.ruling: 65 kg distractor replaced with 75 kg so only the keyed option is under 70% of 1RM.

findings.claim: The Key Fact lists nine component-to-test pairs and its revision tip says “Check your list against the nine tests”.
findings.truth: Muscular endurance and its named test (the Sit-Up Bleep Test) appear in the body text but are missing from the summary box a student revises from. Options: (a) leave it, since the test appears earlier in the lesson; (b) add 'muscular endurance to Sit-Up Bleep Test' to the box and change 'nine tests' to 'ten components'. Recommend (b).
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.3.2 names eleven tests across ten components, including muscular endurance – Sit-Up Bleep Test.
findings.ruling: Added muscular endurance -> Sit-Up Bleep Test to the Key Fact and revision tip; 'nine tests' -> 'ten components'.

findings.claim: “Six structural features of the alveoli are specifically designed to maximise ... First ... Second ... Third ... Fourth ...”
findings.truth: The sentence promises six features and then numbers four, although all six spec ideas sit inside those four (thin walls carries short diffusion distance; capillaries carries large blood supply). Confusing to count from, but nothing stated is wrong.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.1.2 gaseous exchange bullet list.

findings.claim: The interval-training mark scheme credits “ATP-PCr (anaerobic) system”; L14 repeats “the anaerobic ATP-PCr system”.
findings.truth: This specification covers aerobic and anaerobic exercise only; named energy systems are A-level content. Not wrong, but it implies a student needs a term that is not examinable here.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.1.3 (anaerobic and aerobic exercise) names no energy systems.

findings.claim: Hedged mark-scheme attributions left in place: L2 “the mark scheme typically awards 1 mark for each element”, L5 “the mark scheme almost always requires the word 'diffusion'”, L8 “the mark scheme typically awards marks for: writing the formula ...”.
findings.truth: These read as general exam technique rather than invented rubric detail, so they are recorded but not edited. If the programme decides to strip every mark-scheme attribution, these three are the remaining instances.
findings.evidence: house rule on board mark-scheme wording.

summary: Sixteen lessons checked against AQA 8582. Physiology, formulae and every worked calculation (cardiac output, mechanical advantage, heart-rate zones, one rep max, mean, range and percentage change) recompute correctly, and all 80 knowledge-check keys and match orders are right. The real damage sits in L8 (levers): a wrong first-class letter order, a worked example set at the elbow instead of the ankle with both lever arms measured from the wrong point, and a garbled revision tip. L2 reverses the press-up phases, L3 swaps the cricket-bowling and javelin movement examples, L11 has the Ruler Drop set-up back to front, and L10 mislabels a sprinter's components and names a non-AQA component in a mnemonic. Fabricated mark-scheme and examiner claims were rewritten in the house voice.
